lesson.title: Finding angles, and splitting a force

interactive.brief: The one thing you should see is the arrow's floor shadow, F cos θ, and wall shadow, F sin θ, trading length as you turn it, and θ coming back by tan⁻¹ when you drag the shadows.
interactive.title: The arrow and its shadows
interactive.whatAmILookingAt: A short lesson in fifteen small screens. The first eight use lesson 1's right-angled triangle, with θ at the bottom left, the side names in small labels, and a calculator beside it that shows the keys pressed and the answer. Screen 1 is the 150 mm conduit offset with 300 mm between the bends: sin θ = 150 ÷ 300 = 0.5, and the calculator keys sin⁻¹ 0.5 and shows 30°, while an arrow on the picture runs from the ratio back to the angle. Screen 3 sets each inverse key beside the pair of sides it takes, then lays the triangle under the line y = 0.5x, drawn with the same scale on both axes, where rise ÷ run is the gradient, 0.5, and tan⁻¹ 0.5 gives 26.6°. Screen 5 builds two triangles whose ratios need no calculator: half a square with sides 1, 1 and √2, and half an equilateral triangle of side 2, cut down the middle so its 60° top angle splits into two 30° angles, with sides 1, √3 and 2, its height found by Pythagoras as √(4 − 1). Screen 7 puts sin⁻¹ 0.5 = 30° and 1 ÷ sin 30° = 2.0 side by side, an angle and a number, under the names cosec, sec and cot for one over sin, cos and tan. Screen 9 swings the offset's 300 mm of conduit down onto the floor with a dashed arc: it reaches past the run, the side next to 30°, and the piece beyond, the hypotenuse minus the run, is the shrink. From screen 10 the picture is the arrow and its shadows. A force arrow of fixed length F starts from the corner where a floor meets a wall, at angle θ above the floor, and dragging its tip turns it from 0° to 90°. Its shadow on the floor, as if lit from straight above, and its shadow on the wall, as if lit from straight across, are drawn as the two short sides of a right-angled triangle with the arrow as its hypotenuse, labelled F cos θ and F sin θ with their values in newtons. The floor shadow is the side next to θ, so it is F × cos θ, and the wall shadow is the side opposite θ, so it is F × sin θ. Turning the arrow up shortens the floor shadow and lengthens the wall shadow, as more of the arrow goes into its height, while the arrow keeps its length. A switch runs it backwards: drag the ends of the two shadows and the arrow swings to fit, with θ read out as tan⁻¹(wall ÷ floor), because the wall shadow is opposite θ and the floor shadow next to it, and F as √(floor² + wall²), which is Pythagoras. Screen 12 adds a tilt handle that turns the floor into a slope at angle α, with a block on it and its weight W drawn straight down. The shadows now lie along the slope and square to it. On flat ground the line square to the floor points straight down, along the weight; tilting the floor by α tilts that line by α as well, so the weight is α away from it, and its parts are W sin α down the slope and W cos α into it. Some screens show an idea and the rest ask you to try it: a puzzle offers three answers, a wrong pick gets a one-line hint naming its slip, and Why? draws the answer on the picture.
interactive.ignores: The forces, weights, lengths and angles are example figures chosen so the working shows clearly; only the 100 N at 30° is a source's own example. Most answers are rounded to one decimal place, while the working keeps every figure. The arrow turns only from 0° to 90°, as angles past 90° are a later lesson. The block on the slope is drawn with its weight alone, with no friction or other force, because the screen only splits the weight into parts; it does not say whether the block slides.

explain.text:
Lesson 1 went from an angle to a side. This lesson runs it backwards, from two sides to the angle, and then uses the same triangle to split a force into two parts. Remember the 150 mm offset with 300 mm between the bends. The offset depth is the opposite side and the distance between bends the hypotenuse,[^3] so sin θ = 150 ÷ 300 = 0.5. Which angle has a sine of 0.5? The calculator's sin⁻¹ key answers that: sin⁻¹ 0.5 = 30°. It is read [[inverse sine]], because it undoes sin: it is f⁻¹ from Functions and their graphs, the machine run backwards. An inverse takes the output and does the opposite to get back to the input:[^4] sin turns 30° into 0.5, and sin⁻¹ turns 0.5 back into 30°. cos⁻¹ and tan⁻¹ undo cos and tan in the same way. Choose the key as you chose the ratio in lesson 1, from the two sides you have: sine is opposite over hypotenuse, cosine adjacent over hypotenuse, and tangent opposite over adjacent,[^5] so those pairs take sin⁻¹, cos⁻¹ and tan⁻¹. A slope is the last kind. As in Straight-line graphs, its gradient m is rise ÷ run. The rise is the side opposite the slope's angle and the run is the side next to it, so tan θ = m, and the line y = 0.5x, drawn with the same scale on both axes, climbs at tan⁻¹ 0.5 = 26.6°. In a right-angled triangle θ is between 0° and 90°, and that is the angle these keys give; a later lesson finds a second angle with the same sine. You need an inverse key only when you want an angle. A side comes from plain sin, cos or tan and a rearrangement, as in lesson 1.

On sin, cos and tan, ⁻¹ means undo. That is not how Powers and roots read it, where 2⁻¹ is 1 ÷ 2, so it is worth saying twice: sin⁻¹ 0.5 is an angle, 30°, while 1 ÷ sin 30° is a number, 2.0. One over a ratio has a name of its own. 1 ÷ sin θ is the [[cosecant]] of θ, written cosec θ, and it is lesson 1's conduit multiplier, 2.0 at 30° and 1.414 at 45°.[^1] The other two of the six ratios are the secant, sec θ = 1 ÷ cos θ, and the cotangent, cot θ = 1 ÷ tan θ.[^9][^10] A sine is opposite ÷ hypotenuse, and the opposite side is never longer than the hypotenuse, so no angle has a sine above 1, and sin⁻¹ 45 gives an error. Two triangles give exact ratios without a calculator. Cut a square with sides of 1 from corner to corner and each half has two sides of 1 and two equal angles sharing 90°, so 45° each, and by Pythagoras a hypotenuse of √2, so sin 45° = cos 45° = 1/√2, which is 0.7071.[^1] An equilateral triangle has three equal sides and three equal angles, and the angles make 180°, so each is 60°. Take one with sides of 2 and cut it down the middle. The cut halves the top angle into two of 30° and the base into two of 1, so each half has a hypotenuse of 2, a base of 1, and a height of √(4 − 1) = √3. So sin 30° = 1/2, cos 30° = √3/2, which is 0.866, and the two swap for 60°. The same triangles give an offset's [[shrink]]. The 300 mm of conduit between the bends is the hypotenuse, but along the wall it covers only the run, the side next to 30°, 300 × cos 30° = 259.8 mm. So the shrink is 300 − 259.8 = 40.2 mm, or 0.268 for each unit of offset, which is exactly 2 − √3 from the half equilateral triangle's sides of 2, √3 and 1. Field tables round it to 3/16 or 1/4 per inch of offset at 30°,[^13][^14] and treat it as "a common field allowance, not a code rule".[^15]

A force has a size and a direction, so draw it as an arrow: its length is the size and its tilt the direction. Stand it at θ above the floor, and its shadow on the floor and its shadow on the wall are the two short sides of a right-angled triangle, with the arrow as the hypotenuse. The floor shadow is next to θ, so it is F cos θ, and the wall shadow is opposite θ, so it is F sin θ. For a force at an angle above the horizontal, the cosine gives the horizontal part and the sine the vertical part.[^6] A 100 N force at 30° has 100 × cos 30° = 86.6 N along the floor and 100 × sin 30° = 50.0 N up the wall.[^2] These two parts are the force's [[components]]. Together they push exactly as the one force does, so the force can be swapped for its two parts,[^11] and finding them is called resolving the force. Turn the arrow up and the floor shadow shortens while the wall shadow grows, as more of the arrow's length goes into its height. Resolving a force into horizontal and vertical components, for angles from 0° to 90°, is in the MCA's General Engineering Science syllabus.[^7] A launch at an angle splits the same way: its speed has a part across and a part up,[^12] which is the launch Quadratics and polynomials left for here. Run it backwards and the shadows give the angle. The wall shadow is opposite θ and the floor shadow next to it, so wall ÷ floor is tan θ, and tan⁻¹(50 ÷ 86.6) = 30°. Pythagoras gives the arrow back, √(86.6² + 50²) = 100 N. Tilt the floor into a slope at angle α and the same split works along the slope and square to it. A block's weight W still points straight down. On flat ground the line square to the floor points straight down too, along the weight. Tilting the floor by α tilts that line by α as well, so the weight is α away from it. Its part pressing into the slope is the side next to α, W cos α, and its part pulling down the slope is the side opposite, W sin α: for 500 N on 20°, 469.8 N and 171.0 N.

When a second step uses the angle, keep the whole angle in the calculator. A slope rising 1.2 m over a 5 m run is at tan⁻¹ 0.24 = 13.4957…°, and a 600 N crate on it has 600 × sin 13.4957…° = 140.0 N pulling down the slope; round the angle to 13° first and you get 135.0 N. **sin⁻¹, cos⁻¹ and tan⁻¹ undo sin, cos and tan, turning two sides back into an angle,[^4] and a force F at θ above the floor splits into F cos θ along the floor and F sin θ up the wall.[^6]**

analogy.text: A diagonal cable run can be given as one length at an angle, or as how far along and how far up it goes. A run 4 m along and 3 m up is a diagonal of √(4² + 3²) = 5 m at tan⁻¹(3 ÷ 4) = 36.9°. A force splits the same way: its arrow is the diagonal, and its two shadows are the along and the up. Reading the angle back from the along and the up is the inverse key.
analogy.breaks: Running a cable along and then up uses 4 + 3 = 7 m, more than the 5 m diagonal, because the two runs come one after the other. A force's two parts act at the same time in different directions, so they are not added as plain numbers: 86.6 N and 50.0 N would make 136.6 N, yet together they push exactly as the one 100 N arrow does.[^11]

practice.text:
- To find an angle, mark the right angle and θ, and name the two sides you know from θ.
- Choose the key from those two sides: opposite and hypotenuse take sin⁻¹, adjacent and hypotenuse cos⁻¹, opposite and adjacent tan⁻¹.
- Key in the inverse key with the two sides divided inside it, such as sin⁻¹(6 ÷ 10), with the calculator in degrees mode.[^8]
- To split a force, measure θ from the floor, or from the slope. The part along that line is F cos θ, and the part square to it is F sin θ.[^6]
- Check: neither part is longer than F, and √(floor² + wall²) gives F back.

**Rule of thumb:** Want an angle, use an inverse key. Want a side, use plain sin, cos or tan and rearrange.

**Worked example:** A winch rope pulls a skid with an example 800 N at 15° above the floor. Along the floor: 800 × cos 15° = 772.7 N. Up from the floor: 800 × sin 15° = 207.1 N. As a check, run it backwards: tan⁻¹(207.1 ÷ 772.7) = 15.0°, and √(772.7² + 207.1²) = 800 N.

**Common mistakes**
- Reading sin⁻¹ as one over sin. sin⁻¹ 0.6 is an angle, 36.9°, while 1 ÷ 0.6 is 1.67, a number. One over sin is the cosecant, the conduit multiplier.[^1]
- The wrong inverse key. With opposite 6 and hypotenuse 10, cos⁻¹ 0.6 gives 53.1°, the triangle's other angle.
- Measuring θ from the wall. Then cos and sin swap: F cos θ is always the part along the line θ is measured from.
- Rounding in the middle. Rounding 13.4957° to 13° turns a 140.0 N answer into 135.0 N.
- Keying in a side or an angle where a ratio belongs, such as sin⁻¹ 45. No sine is more than 1, so the calculator shows an error: divide the two sides first.

interactive.title: The arrow and its shadows
interactive.brief: The one thing you should see is the arrow's floor shadow, F cos θ, and wall shadow, F sin θ, trading length as you turn it, and θ coming back by tan⁻¹ when you drag the shadows.

checks.label: An inverse function takes the output and does the opposite to get back to the input: on the first screen sin takes 30° to 0.5, the calculator keys sin⁻¹ of the drawn 150 ÷ 300 = 0.5 and gives back 30, the angle the triangle is drawn at, and sin⁻¹ undoes sin at every whole angle from 0° to 90°

When you bend an offset the conduit forms a right triangle, the offset depth the vertical (opposite) side and the distance between bends the diagonal (hypotenuse): the first screen marks 150 mm on the upright opposite side and 300 mm on the diagonal hypotenuse, drawn to one scale with a square corner

Sine is the ratio of the opposite side to the hypotenuse, cosine the adjacent side to the hypotenuse, and tangent the opposite side to the adjacent side: on the keys screen sin⁻¹, cos⁻¹ and tan⁻¹ each light exactly that pair of sides, and every angle puzzle's answer is the inverse of that ratio of its drawn sides

Scientific calculators should be in degrees mode for trigonometry: every calculator drawn, on every screen and in every answer state, is marked DEG, and its inverse key gives degrees, sin⁻¹ 0.5 = 30 where radians would give 0.524

For 30 degrees sin(30) = 0.5, so the cosecant is 1/0.5 = 2.0; for 45 degrees sin(45) = 0.7071, so the cosecant is 1/0.7071 = 1.414: the calculators show 1 ÷ sin 30 = 2 and 1 ÷ sin 45 = 1.414, worked out as one over sin, beside sin⁻¹ 0.5 = 30, an angle

A 100 N force at 30 degrees has Fx = 100 N • cos 30° = 86.6 N and Fy = 100 N • sin 30° = 50.0 N: the arrow screen opens at 100 N and 30° with exactly these on its floor and wall shadows, each measured off the drawn arrow

To find the vertical component of a force the sine function can be used, and for the horizontal component the cosine: at every whole angle from 0° to 90° the wall shadow is the drawn arrow's height and reads F sin θ, the floor shadow its width and reads F cos θ, and turning the arrow up shortens the floor shadow and lengthens the wall shadow while the arrow keeps its length

Resolve forces in horizontal and vertical components restricted to the first quadrant: dragging the arrow's tip anywhere turns it no further than 0° or 90°, so neither shadow is ever negative, and run backwards each shadow stays between 5 N and 100 N

Run backwards, the shadows give the arrow back: for every pair of shadows, the arrow is drawn from the corner to the point they mark, with the handles on the shadows' ends, θ reads tan⁻¹(wall ÷ floor) and F reads √(floor² + wall²); switching from 100 N at 30° gives back 30.0° and 100.0 N

On the slope the weight W points straight down and its parts lie along the slope and square to it: at every whole tilt from 0° to 40° the part down the slope is W sin α and the part into it W cos α, both measured off the drawing, the weight is α away from the line square to the slope, and 500 N on 20° gives 171.0 N and 469.8 N

The line y = 0.5x is drawn with the same scale on both axes: the ticks on both axes are the same distance apart, the line climbs 0.5 for each 1 across, the triangle under it has rise ÷ run = 0.5 measured off the drawing, and its angle is tan⁻¹ 0.5 = 26.6°

Shrink is the conduit between the bends, the hypotenuse, less the run along the wall: on the shrink screen the run measured off the drawing is 300 × cos 30° = 259.8 mm, the piece of swung-down conduit beyond it is 300 − 259.8 = 40.2 mm, and that is 0.268 a millimetre of offset, exactly 2 − √3, against the rounded field figures of 3/16 and 1/4 per inch
Each puzzle accepts only its right answer, every wrong answer has its own hint and its own red row of working, and before an answer nothing in the picture shows the answer

No label sits on another label, a line or a handle, or runs off the picture, on any screen in any state: puzzles answered right, wrong or with Why? open, the arrow at every angle and run backwards at its smallest and largest shadows, the slope at every tilt
Every demonstration has finished within 4.5 s of its screen opening, none starting before the 0.35 s screen fade ends; each answer, Why? and switch has settled within 1.8 s

applied.problem: "Divide the two sides, then press the inverse key" does not work as written on common natural-display calculators, where sin⁻¹ opens a bracket that needs the ratio inside it; keying sin⁻¹(6 ÷ 10) works on any of them.

Says answers are rounded to one decimal place, but the lesson also shows 1.67, 0.7071, 1.414, 0.866, 24° and 66°, and 13.4957° deliberately unrounded, so the blanket rule is not true of its own figures.
